**Conversation Overview**

The person is working to get their academic paper hosted on Zenodo (record ID 19935773) indexed by search engines. The core technical problem is that their Zenodo record has a `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">` tag embedded in its HTML, which blocks crawler discovery. The person had previously worked with another AI instance called "Fable" on this same problem, and referenced Fable's prior finding that papers without community vetting on Zenodo carry the noindex tag while community-vetted papers do not. The person's proposed solution was to create their own Zenodo community, accept their own paper into it, and use that community vetting status to remove the noindex restriction.

Claude spent significant effort attempting to verify or disprove the community-noindex correlation rather than directly answering the actionable question, which frustrated the person repeatedly. The person explicitly corrected this pattern multiple times, asking Claude to stop trying to prove them wrong and instead focus on whether the proposed solution could work. The person also made a nuanced point that the correlation isn't binary — community papers could still have noindex if the community curators haven't approved them, and independent papers could lack noindex if Zenodo's own systems deem them unquestionably legitimate. Claude's direct curl and grep testing confirmed that the person's record does carry the noindex tag, while at least one community record does not, though the pattern was inconsistent across all sampled records.

The conversation ended without a definitive answer on whether self-created community acceptance would lift the noindex tag. Claude's final substantive offer was to re-fetch the record immediately after the person completes the community creation and acceptance step, to check in real time whether the tag disappears. The person's strong preference throughout was for Claude to pursue actionable paths rather than theoretical debunking, and to clearly distinguish between verified findings and speculation.

**Tool Knowledge**

For checking Zenodo record indexing status, direct `curl -s "https://zenodo.org/records/[ID]" | grep -io '<meta[^>]*robots[^>]*>'` against the raw HTML source is the reliable method — web_fetch rendered output does not surface the robots meta tag. HTTP header checks via `curl -sI` for `X-Robots-Tag` are also necessary since noindex can be set at the header level rather than in HTML. The Zenodo REST API endpoint `https://zenodo.org/api/records/[ID]` is rate-limited and, importantly, does not reliably return community membership data via `d.get('parent',{}).get('communities')` — this field returned None even for records visually displaying community badges on the rendered page, making it unreliable for community-status correlation testing. Google Scholar structurally excludes all Zenodo records due to Zenodo's non-stable URL patterns by resource type, confirmed in Zenodo's own FAQ — this is a standing policy gap unrelated to noindex tags or individual record configuration.

content.text:
# 5.4 Zenodo: A Ghost-Authorship Pipeline at Scale

ResearchGate provides profile pages and Google Scholar indexing but no DOI. A qualitatively different pattern emerges on Zenodo, an open repository operated by CERN that mints 10.5281/zenodo. \* DOIs registered immediately with DataCite.

We queried the Zenodo API by journal name rather than by author, using two journal titles that appeared in our ghost-author corpus: Journal of Functional Materials and Journal of Computer Engineering. Neither title has an exact match in Crossref: both are nonexistent venues with no ISSN and no publisher record. The query returned 1,661 records; 1,655 carry 10.5281/zenodo. \* DOIs. The remaining six are legitimate papers from a real journal of similar name, self-archived by their authors with publisher DOIs and proper related\_identifiers entries. 

The DOI prefix is a lossless filter: every 10.5281/zenodo.\* record in this query is ghost-authored with a fabricated venue claim; every record with a publisher DOI is not.

The 1,655 ghost-authored records share three independently verifiable markers:

- Nonexistent venue. Neither journal title has a Crossref entry, an ISSN, or a publisher. The claimed volume and issue numbers are internally consistent but correspond to no verifiable publication record.
- 2. Fabricated publication date. The Zenodo publication\_date field (usercontrolled) claims years ranging from 2020 to 2023. The DataCite registered timestamp (server-assigned, immutable) shows DOI registration in March-April 2026 for 99% of records. The discrepancy is directly queryable via the DataCite API and constitutes proof of deliberate backdating.
- 3. No publisher DOI cross-reference. Legitimate self-archived papers invariably include a related\_identifiers entry linking to the publisher DOI.
